messages.body_plain:
> You're right, the sample is small and that is causing problems of convergence. However, it also seems like Lavaan doesn't like ordered variables much.

I have never heard lavaan express that sentiment.  I have fit large latent-variable models with dozens of ordinal variables before.  I would be more inclined to think the optimizer has a hard time searching a parameter space when it doesn't have enough information from the data to tell it where search for good estimates.

> Does SEM cope well with unequal sizes? The Tperception variable, for example, has 16 numeric observations and 13 NAs.

Unequal sizes of what?  You don't need uniformly distributed categories, but you do need more data.  According to your picture, the Tperception variable isn't numeric, it is a factor with 6 observed categories (named "8", "12", "1", "2", "3", and "(Other)"), most of which only have 1 or 2 observations per category.  You can't even trust a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test on a one-way table with such disparate data, much less a large-sample technique like a common-factor model.  And is Tperception even an ordered factor, or is it just nominal?  lavaan only handles ordered categorical indicators, with binary as a special case.  Use the class() function to see how your variables are being treated in your data.frame, and redefine your variables using the ordered() function if necessary and appropriate.

> How should I approach the model if I want to include more than one ordered variable?

There was nothing wrong with your model syntax.  You just don't have enough data to fit this model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

You can build a model however you think is appropriate, e.g., based on substantive theory and past research if you are doing confirmatory research, or progressively using data-driven techniques if you are doing exploratory research. Regression textbooks typically have some discussion on model building.  If you have actual lavaan questions or problems, you can post your syntax to this group for help.  But because you say you aren't running a multilevel model (apparently estimating fixed effects of "subject" instead of random effects, for whatever reason), it would be more appropriate to post your questions about lavaan syntax in a new thread instead of replying to this one.

messages.body_plain:
On 05/02/2016 08:40 PM, Mariella Sciortino wrote:
> Dear Yves,
>
> Could you kindly give me a reference to the theory behind why
> MLM estimation requires mean structure please?

For MLM, as far as I can tell, a meanstructure is not needed in theory.
This is just an implementational issue: in lavaan, the (old) code for
the Satorra-Bentler test statistic insists on having a meanstructure.

The new code (which is not used yet in 0.5-20), does not need this
anymore. You can try this out by fitting a model with no meanstructure,
and estimator = "ML", and then type:

lavaan:::lav_test_satorra_bentler(fit)$satorra.benter

Once the 'old' functions get replaced by the 'new' functions, this
limitation will go away.

Then again, using a meanstructure never hurts.

Yves.

messages.subject: dwls & standard errors
messages.subject_clean: dwls & standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was studying the dwls estimator in lavaan and was struck by the influence model size has on the standard errors. Using the package simsem and the available vignettes I ran a model with four binary indicators and then another with 12 binary indicators. The standard errors increased a lot. With the 12 item bias exceeds 30% for nearly all or all standard errors while the four item model bias remained unremarkable (< .05). Similar results are obtained when the thresholds are increased to two. What struck me about this is the literature seems to suggests the DWLS is able to maintain nominal levels of bias for the standard errors (e.g., Forero et al., 2009). Sensitivity of the estimated standard errors to model size seems to be more consistent with WLS (e.g., Flora et al., 2004).

I guess I am wondering what I am miss-understanding.

Thanks for any insight.
John

Forero, C. G., Maydeu-Olivares, A., & Gallardo-Pujol, D. (2009). Factor analysis with ordinal indicators: A Monte Carlo study comparing DWLS and ULS estimation. Structural Equation Modeling, 16(4), 625-641.

Flora, D. B., & Curran, P. J. (2004). An empirical evaluation of alternative methods of estimation for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data.Psychological methods, 9(4), 466.

messages.subject: Re: dwls & standard errors
messages.subject_clean: dwls & standard errors
messages.body_plain:
An increase in overidentifying degrees of freedom leads to an increase
in small sample biases. That's a finding known in theoretical
econometrics literature, not only through simulations, but through
methodological derivations as well -- although any general second
order asymptotics is freaking difficult, so the models that
econometricians looked at were somewhat simplified.

If you are running DWLS on the sample covariance matrix of the binary
items and hope to obtain some "robustness" advertised for DWLS, I
think you may be in there for a long haul. Even though DWLS ignores
the cross-covariances responsible for the (violations of) multivariate
normality, it still hopes, deep in its heart, that the data are
multivariate normal, in the sense that the second order moments are
all that you need. However, the more binary indicators you drop into
your model, the farther you will be from multivariate normality. Even
if you work on the polychoric correlations matrix, you only improve
things by a small bit: the polychoric correlations may not be
identified well with small cells. The standard errors on these
correlations can be sizeable, and asymptotics may not work well for
them.

I am just thinking aloud here, I don't have very concrete answers.

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)
-- Principal Survey Scientist, Abt SRBI
-- Education Officer, Survey Research Methods Section of the American
Statistical Association
-- Opinions stated in this email are mine only, and do not reflect the
position of my employer
-- http://stas.kolenikov.name

messages.subject_clean: Controlling for the influence of independent variables in MG-SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

thank you very much for your detailed answer.

Am Freitag, 15. April 2016 11:47:18 UTC+2 schrieb Terrence Jorgensen:
> > I want to control for the influence of the variable "Doku" (just like in a "classical" ANCOVA) while testing for group differences on the dependent variables. Is it correct to regress them onto the variable "Doku"? Compared to a model without the regression, the means are adjusted. Of course, lavaan will estimated the regression coefficients freely across the groups. Is that meaningful? I do have a theoretical justification, but as far as I know this is not done in ANCOVA, right? I think that covariates in ANCOVA should actually be equal across groups...
>
> Yes, you are referring to the "assumption" of homogeneous slopes/hyperplanes in ANCOVA.  In order to test group-differences in adjusted means (or equivalently, group-differences in intercepts in a regression model), the distance between 2 groups' regression lines need to be constant across all levels of the covariate (Doku).  If there is an interaction between Doku and Group, then the lines are not parallel, so group differences are larger at some levels of Doku than at other levels of Doku.  In this case, there is no single valid test of difference in adjusted means or intercepts; instead, you would probe the interaction by testing group-mean differences at multiple meaningful levels of Doku (e.g., the observed minimum, maximum, and median, or the Mean + / - SD, or any levels of Doku that are substantively interesting "subpopulations" to compare).  You do this by centering Doku at each of the chosen levels and running your model(s) again, so that "Doku == 0" represents that centered value.  This works because in the presence of an interaction, the test of a difference in group intercepts (i.e., the effect of Group) is conditional on the moderator (Doku) being held constant at zero.
>
> In the context of a multiple-group CFA/MIMIC model, Group implicitly interacts with every predictor (in your case, Doku and latent factors) because slopes are freely estimated across groups.  In fact, the test of metric (or "weak") invariance is a test of the interaction between Group and the latent factor(s) on the outcomes/indicators.  I will also point out that because you are interested in testing for group-differences in latent intercepts, you need to assume not only that the latent factors are measured invariably across groups, but also that the latent factors are measured invariably across levels of Doku.  If Doku is a continuous variable, you can test invariance using the MIMIC method.  Basically, fit a series of configural-invariance models (i.e., free estimates across groups) in which Doku predicts not only the latent factors but also one indicator per factor, and test whether the effect of Doku on each indicator is zero after controlling for the effect of the latent factor.  You will have to test all indicators, so use a Bonferroni-adjusted alpha level for the number of indicators you test.  If any are significant in either group, include those effects in your configural model when you start to test invariance across groups.  For a valid test of scalar (or "strong") invariance, you will first need to test whether the effects of Doku on any indicators differ across groups (i.e., whether Group and Doku interact in their effects on indicators -- this is testing the assumption of homogenous slopes across groups for the measurement model).  It doesn't matter whether you test the equality of "indicator ~ Doku" effects before or after testing metric invariance, but I would do them in separate steps because they are distinct null hypotheses.  If any Doku effects on indicators exist, and they cannot be constrained across groups, then you have to test partial scalar invariance across groups (i.e., don't constrain intercepts across groups for those indicators).
>
> Back to your original question -- Assuming you have at least partial measurement invariance with respect to Group and to Doku, then you need to test whether the effects of Doku on latent factors are equal across groups.

How do I accomplish this? Do I estimate two models with the arguments group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts") and group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "regression") and compare if the latter fits significantly worse - if so I do assume that the effect of Doku is not equal across groups?

and

> If none differ, then there is no evidence of an interaction, so you can finally test group-differences in latent intercepts while controlling for Doku (same as testing group-differences in adjusted means in ANCOVA).

This is done by evaluating the mean structure of  the latter model group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "regressions") , right?

> However, if any effects of Doku on latent variables differ across groups, then you would need to probe the Group-Doku interaction by testing group-mean differences at some meaningful levels of Doku (use centering, as described in the first paragraph).
>

Once again, thank you very much!
Tobias
>

messages.body_plain:
> Do I estimate two models with the arguments group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts") and group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "regression") and compare if the latter fits significantly worse - if so I do assume that the effect of Doku is not equal across groups?

Yes, assuming those are the only regression parameters in your model (besides "loadings").  But it might be safer to explicitly label the regression parameters you want to constrain (e.g., 'int ~ c(beta1, beta1)*Doku'), assigning different labels to each group in the unconstrained model (e.g., 'int ~ c(beta1, beta2)*Doku').

> This is done by evaluating the mean structure of  the latter model group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "regressions") , right?

Yes, but again, I would recommend labeling regression parameters and latent intercepts in the syntax so you know exactly what you are constraining.  The "intercepts" in the group.equal argument refer only to observed indicators.  Latent variables would be "means", but that is confusing because your latent variables will be endogenous, so the means aren't actually estimated.  You can specify and label the latent intercepts by regressing the latent factors on 1 (e.g.,  'int ~ c(int.intercept1, int.intercept2)*1').

> I am trying to figure out if I can add quadratic and/or polynomial terms within a path model in lavaan.

If you want to include nonlinearity in variables (e.g., interaction terms or polynomials), then you need to calculate those nonlinear variables manually and add them to your data.frame, then use add those variables as predictors in your lavaan syntax.  For example:

> myData$x.squ <- myData$x^2
> myData$x.cub <- myData$x^3
>
> syntax <- ' y ~ x + x.squ + x.cub '

dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8

f2 <- f2 - mean(f2)

messages.subject_clean: Adding Quadratic Term in a Path Model?
messages.body_plain:
> I am interested how lavaan calculates degrees of freedom and what the implications are for only having one degree of freedom in this model.

As with other modeling frameworks, df are calculated as the difference between the observed and estimated pieces of information, but in covariance structure analysis the observed pieces of information are not the rows of data.  Rather, they are the observed sample  moments (variances, covariances, and optionally means).  When you add the polynomial terms, those variables will be separate rows/columns in your covariance matrix and mean vector, too.  Unless you set "fixed.x = FALSE", then the submatrix of exogenous variables is treated as fixed rather than estimated, so don't count those cells when calculating df.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> I wish to ensure that my data and the path model used to fit the data meet the assumptions of linearity, normally distributed errors, and homogeneity of variance.

In covariance structure analysis, "residuals" are differences between observed and expected (model-implied, predicted) elements of the covariance matrix, not differences between observed and expected values of the outcome(s) for each row of data.  If you want to do that kind of residual analysis (assuming you only have observed variables in your path analysis), you can either use the estimates to calculate predicted values and then residuals, or you can just fit a regression model to each outcome and extract the residuals like you would after running regressions using lm().

messages.subject: Re: Weird error (bug?)
messages.subject_clean: Weird error (bug?)
messages.body_plain:
I came across a similar error and suspect it is related to specifying residual correlations that involve an exogenous variable (where fixed.x=FALSE). This is probably not the best example (and perhaps the m2 syntax is "illegal"), but see below.

set.seed(1002)
dat <- data.frame(matrix(rnorm(550), 50, 11))
names(dat) <- paste("y", 1:11, sep="")

m1 <- '
  lv1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
  lv2 =~ y5

  lv2 ~ lv1

  y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
'

## equivalent to m1?
m2 <- '
  lv1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4

  y5 ~ lv1

  y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
'

## m1 runs but does not converge:
fit1 <- sem(m1, data=dat)
## m2 gives "parameter not defined" error:
fit2 <- sem(m2, data=dat, fixed.x=FALSE)

And m2 runs if you remove the y1 ~~ y5 covariance.

messages.body_plain:
Hello-

I am completing a CFA and would like to compare measurement variance across two groups. I have a very elementary understanding of what the measurementinvariance output represents and would appreciate some clarification in how I am interpreting the following output. Am I correct to conclude that

1) configural invariance holds: i.e. the two groups have identical number and type of factors and same set of significant loadings [This is the part that I am most unclear on. If the factor structures differed for the two groups, how would the output signal this?]

2) despite the significant chi-square diff tests, the Delta-CFI may support strong variance using <.01 cut off; while only configural invariance holds applying the <.002 cut off? (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/FQ5EWmclbjI/z3Dtv4Z5AAAJ)

Many thanks

> strong=cfa(MODEL, data=Data, group="gp", group.equal = c("loadings","intercepts"))

Hi

Regression factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, and not just the indicators of one factor. If you compare my example with yours, you can see that I did not subset the indicator covariance matrix like you do. That should explain the different results.

But let’s take a step back: What is it that you really want to do? Do you want to calculate factor scores or do you want to calculate some kind of model-based predictions. These are two different things. If you want to predict, what exactly are you predicting and with what?

Mikko

Hmmm...yes i think this will be a better way to go about. I'll tell you the premise: I have a client for whom I am modeling churn using SEM. Now the client is not very 'analytics savy' and wants to be sure why/how SEM is different from the predictions I would have made from logistic or decision trees. So, I have namely, three goals here:
Predicting observations using SEM coefficients (both measurement and structural model) and looking at the overall accuracy - Here, basically I have some X's (observed predictor manifest variables) and Y's (observed predicted manifest variables). Additionally, I want to predict the Y's by forming a set of mathematical linear equations of the model using the coefficients from R.
Comparing Factor Scores to gauge the importance of different observed variables/underlying factors : Here, I want to compare the factor scores from R output to compare different observed variables as well as factors in predicting Y. However, this is the next objective and I will come to this later in the thread
Benchmarking the prediction accuracy and factor contribution with the results of logistic as well as decision trees
I do know I can compare the various GOF indices and inturn compare the results of these techniques. But, as I mentioned, the client is not very comfortable with various statistical terms, hence, he wants the entire discussion to be more around the 'easily interpretable' regression coefficients and mathematical equations. This brings us to my first question on the thread as to how can we predict the output using R coefficients from the lavaan package (J)

I am not sure if I communicated everything clearly but do let me know if you want to know anything else

And thanks in advance

messages.subject: Re: Making sense of measurement invariance output: What does fit.configural output mean?
messages.subject_clean: Making sense of measurement invariance output: What does fit.configural output mean?
messages.body_plain:
> Given the absolute fit of the configural model, does the following result indicate that the configural invariance does not exist (also, rmsea does exceed .06 (.062)? If this is the case, should the conclusion be that: the two groups do not have identical number and type of factors and/or the same set of significant loadings? I remain a bit unclear on the interpretation of the output, specifically pertaining to the significance of the configural invariance.

There is no simple diagnosis for why a configural model does not fit well.  It could be that the cross-loadings or correlated residuals exists in one group but not another, which would only necessitate freeing parameter but retaining the same basic structure.  But as you suggested, it might also indicate the groups have fundamentally different factor structures.

Interestingly, the fit of the configural model does not just reflect group differences in model structure, but also overall model fit.  That is, you might have mediocre model fit, but the model might be equally (in)appropriate in both groups.  The semTools packages also has a function called permuteMeasEq(), which uses permutation methods to test configural invariance without confounding that test with overall model fit.  But that method has not yet been investigated much, so it is not clear whether you should try to address the overall fit of the model before or after testing configural invariance.  If you have any theoretically driven reasons to free certain parameters or posit competing models for your data, you should probably try fitting those models before using any data-driven techniques to tweak your model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Standard errors (and confidence intervals) for indirect effect in the std.all solution
messages.subject_clean: Standard errors (and confidence intervals) for indirect effect in the std.all solution
messages.body_plain:
> I'm trying to get the standard errors and confidence intervals for the standardized (std.all) indirect effects of my mediation model.
> I can only obtain the estimate but I cannot figure out a way to obtain se and ci (like for exemple in Mplus when OUTPUT: SDTYX is used)

The usual recommendation is to test null hypotheses about the raw parameters, and just interpret standardized estimates as standardized measures of effect size.  The adjustments to SEs of standardized estimates should lead to the same inferences as the raw parameters' SEs.

> I would like to obtain bootstrapped ci, but this seems difficult since I'm using MLR estimator.

If you want bootstrapped CIs to test null hypotheses, you don't need to adjust the SEs or chi-squared using MLR.  The point estimates in MLR are not adjusted, they are the same as ML estimates.  So you can just use bootstrapped CIs to test parameters and the Bollen-Stine bootstrap for chi-squared.

> If I try to get bootstrap ci using bootstrapLavaan(fit), the output doest not include the defined parameters.

bootstrapLavaan() accepts any function you give it.  So you can just define a function the returns the user-defined parameters from the appropriate rows/column of the standardizedSolution() output, then submit that function to bootstrapLavaan().  See an example in the Details section of the ?bootstrapLavaan help page.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Jesus--
     "Identified at start values" does not mean very much if start values are arbitrary--like getting the weather forecast for some arbitrary location. If you chose meaningful start values and found the model not identified, that could possibly mean something.
     The larger problem that you have is with factor indeterminacy (Guttman 1955). The common factor model has an indeterminacy built into it, so that the factors are partly arbitrary in their values. Each factor is partly a weighted function of the data (this is what you get from the regression method or Bartlett's method or any of the 4 or 5 other methods) and partly a function of an arbitrary vector. Especially when there are few observed variables per common factor, the degree of indeterminacy--the weight given to the arbitrary component--will be quite large. The indeterminacy means that different sets of factor scores can be equally consistent with the same factor model, BUT those different sets of scores need not be highly correlated (or even positively correlated) with each other--because they are largely arbitrary. Particularly given that you do not have many observed variables given the number of common factors, you should give up the notion of finding values for the common factors. You are asking more of the analytical technique than it can provide.
--Ed Rigdon
Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

Just to be clear, that is just a packaged version of inverting the independent variables covariance matrix and multiplying it with the vector of covariance between the independent and dependent variables.

> We know that SEM uses a set of equations (measurement model and structural model) to predict Y.

I do not think that you should think of SEM in terms of prediction, but in terms of explanation. You are trying to explain the relationships between the observed variables with the model.

> For instance, below are the theoretical equations used in the model:
>
> # measurement model
> ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3.....(1)
> dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4.....(2)
> dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8....(3)
> # structural model
> dem60 ~ ind60.....(4)
> dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60....(5)
>
> To get the regression scores for each equation, I will be entering the covariance matrix for each of them and getting the beta coefficients.Is this the right way to go?

Note that these are not five regression equations, but a lot more. A factor such as

ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

means that the factor explains all three indicators, so each indicator has an equation. You do not use the SEM equations to calculate factor scores.

Mikko

On Monday, May 9, 2016 at 2:22:58 PM UTC+2, Edward Rigdon wrote:

> Jesus--
>      "Identified at start values" does not mean very much if start values are arbitrary--like getting the weather forecast for some arbitrary location. If you chose meaningful start values and found the model not identified, that could possibly mean something.
>      The larger problem that you have is with factor indeterminacy (Guttman 1955). The common factor model has an indeterminacy built into it, so that the factors are partly arbitrary in their values. Each factor is partly a weighted function of the data (this is what you get from the regression method or Bartlett's method or any of the 4 or 5 other methods) and partly a function of an arbitrary vector. Especially when there are few observed variables per common factor, the degree of indeterminacy--the weight given to the arbitrary component--will be quite large. The indeterminacy means that different sets of factor scores can be equally consistent with the same factor model, BUT those different sets of scores need not be highly correlated (or even positively correlated) with each other--because they are largely arbitrary. Particularly given that you do not have many observed variables given the number of common factors, you should give up the notion of finding values for the common factors. You are asking more of the analytical technique than it can provide.
> --Ed Rigdon
> Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

Jesus

The problem that I see in your model is that is globally identified (meaning that has positive df), but most constructs are not locally identified. You want to have both, local identification means that each construct its identified by itself, if you were to run a model with only that construct it would be identified to be estimated.

A way to identifed locaaly tour model would be something like this, note that I am adding std.lv <http://std.lv>=T to set the identification by standardizing the latent variables, without it the default is to set by fixing a factor loading to 1.
This code is identifing the constructs with 2 indicators by fixing the 2 factor loading to the same value, this way each construct is just identify

Model148 <- '

W =~ a*GDPCAP + a*TECHINBAND

G =~ b*INSPROPRO + b*PRIMEDUC

C =~ c*ETHICBEHAV + c*IRREPAY

M =~ TECHAVLAT + TECHFIRMABS + FOMASIZE

D =~ W + G + C + M'

fit148 <- sem(Model148, data = Datvarpap8, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)

summary(fit148, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, rsq = TRUE)

messages.subject: Reporting a polychoric correlation matrix in an article - restricted or unrestricted ?
messages.subject_clean: Reporting a polychoric correlation matrix in an article - restricted or unrestricted ?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am doing a questionnaire validation (confirmative) study with skewed data (n = 268), so I used lavaan's MLM estimator. It is my understanding that such an estimator is based on a polychoric correlation matrix (isn't it ?).

In the article Reporting Practices in Confirmatory Factor Analysis: An Overview and Some Recommendations, Jackson et al. (2009) advised to report in CFA papers the correlation matrix for the sake of replication (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19271845).

Based on this example: http://rpackages.ianhowson.com/cran/lavaan/man/lavCor.html, I was able to create such a polychoric correlation matrix with the following commands (5-item scale):

SAS_DATA_ORD <- as.data.frame( lapply(SAS_DATA, cut, 5, labels=FALSE) )
lavCor(SAS_DATA_ORD, ordered=names(SAS_DATA_ORD))

It is my understanding that this set of commands creates a matrix based on an unrestricted model. However, such a correlation matrix would be more suitable for an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) than for a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), since CFA is based on a restricted model.

Therefore, would it be more adequate to report in the article the correlation matrix based on the restricted model that is the aim of the CFA ? How is it possible to create such a polychoric correlation matrix based on my restricted model ?
Is the command inspect(SAS.FIT, "sampstat")$cov appropriate for this ?

I would appreciate any guidance on this subject.

Thank you,

Michael

I guess the answer then is no: You cannot take the SEM equations and calculate predictions of Ys because the Ys are expressed as functions of latent variables and you cannot predict based on something that you cannot observe.

What you can do is to calculate factor scores, and then calculate predictions based on the scores using the SEM equations. The problem with this approach is that the factor scores are calculated based on all indicators, including the one that you want to predict. If your prediction equations require data on the variable being predicted, then prediction would be quite pointless, right?

If you want to do linear predictions using the information from the SEM model, you can use the model implied covariance matrix to calculate the prediction equations.

>
> To conclude, even I believe that mat.regress is not the best way to calculate the regression scores in SEM. Is there some other way I can predict Y's using SEM?

The best way to calculate regression factor scores would be to use lavaan’s predict function. You can do that with matrix algebra (solve and %*%) or with mat.regress as well.

messages.subject: Re: Reporting a polychoric correlation matrix in an article - restricted or unrestricted ?
messages.subject_clean: Reporting a polychoric correlation matrix in an article - restricted or unrestricted ?
messages.body_plain:
> I used lavaan's MLM estimator. It is my understanding that such an estimator is based on a polychoric correlation matrix (isn't it ?).

No, it is regular ML estimation.  Afterward, the standard errors and chi-squared statistic are adjusted as a function of the excess kurtosis of the variables.

> In the article Reporting Practices in Confirmatory Factor Analysis: An Overview and Some Recommendations, Jackson et al. (2009) advised to report in CFA papers the correlation matrix for the sake of replication (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19271845 <http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov%2Fpubmed%2F19271845&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNFIW5T6doZgN-jUyKJxZ68bBHhKKQ>).

You should analyze the covariance matrix.  Fitting the model to the correlation matrix will yield incorrect standard errors.  If you report the correlation matrix, you should also report the SDs for the sake of replication.  Since you are using a robust estimator, you should also report the skew and kurtosis, although I'm not sure whether those univariate statistics would be sufficient to replicate the analysis.

> Based on this example: http://rpackages.ianhowson.com/cran/lavaan/man/lavCor.html, I was able to create such a polychoric correlation matrix with the following commands (5-item scale):
>
> SAS_DATA_ORD <- as.data.frame( lapply(SAS_DATA, cut, 5, labels=FALSE) )
> lavCor(SAS_DATA_ORD, ordered=names(SAS_DATA_ORD))
>
> It is my understanding that this set of commands creates a matrix based on an unrestricted model. However, such a correlation matrix would be more suitable for an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) than for a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), since CFA is based on a restricted model.

EFA is less restricted than CFA because EFA allows all cross-loadings (or as many as possible to identify the model).  But EFA is still imposes some restrictions, which is why the df > 0 (unless it is saturated).  The "unrestricted" model you read about in the ?lavCor help page is just a saturated model, which freely estimates all bivariate correlations.

But you might not need to do this.  Analyzing a polychoric correlation matrix is recommended for binary or ordinal indicators, not for continuous indicators, or at least approximately continuous (e.g., Likert items with at least 7 categories).  And if you have categorical indicators, you don't need to estimate the polychoric correlation matrix.  You just use the "ordered" argument to tell lavaan which variables are categorical, and it will use the appropriate steps by default.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates
messages.subject_clean: Model identification and lavpredict factor score estimates
messages.body_plain:
Jesus,

I think "local identification" is a heuristic.  A model is either globally identified or not, and if it is not, then you look for clues about which part of the model might not be "locally" identified so you can solve the problem.  Identification can depend on aspects of your data, not just counting the number of free parameters and observed sample moments.  A 2-indicator CFA by itself is not identified without the constraints such as the ones you used (or, for example, fixing both factor loadings to 1 and estimating the common factor variance and both unique factor variances).  But when you have multiple 2-indicator constructs in a model, it can be identified (i.e., a unique solution can be found), as long as the constructs correlate.  Steiger illustrates this in the first section of this article:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//1082-989X.7.2.210

I didn't see any evidence of empirical underidentification in your original model, but the model with equal factor loadings fits poorly and yields estimates at the border ("Heywood cases").  So I would recommend trusting the results from the less constrained model in your original post.  But I also agree with Ed that factor score indeterminacy is an important limitation to using factor scores.  If you were planning to use the factor scores in a subsequent model, you would probably be better off just incorporating that model into this model to estimate those parameters (assuming the model is not so large that your small sample size becomes a limiting factor).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

If you report the correlation matrix, you should also report the SDs for the sake of replication.  Since you are using a robust estimator, you should also report the skew and kurtosis, although I'm not sure whether those univariate statistics would be sufficient to replicate the analysis.
>
> > Based on this example: http://rpackages.ianhowson.com/cran/lavaan/man/lavCor.html, I was able to create such a polychoric correlation matrix with the following commands (5-item scale):
> >
> > SAS_DATA_ORD <- as.data.frame( lapply(SAS_DATA, cut, 5, labels=FALSE) )
> > lavCor(SAS_DATA_ORD, ordered=names(SAS_DATA_ORD))
> >
> > It is my understanding that this set of commands creates a matrix based on an unrestricted model. However, such a correlation matrix would be more suitable for an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) than for a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), since CFA is based on a restricted model.
>
> EFA is less restricted than CFA because EFA allows all cross-loadings (or as many as possible to identify the model).  But EFA is still imposes some restrictions, which is why the df > 0 (unless it is saturated).  The "unrestricted" model you read about in the ?lavCor help page is just a saturated model, which freely estimates all bivariate correlations.
>
> But you might not need to do this.  Analyzing a polychoric correlation matrix is recommended for binary or ordinal indicators, not for continuous indicators, or at least approximately continuous (e.g., Likert items with at least 7 categories).  And if you have categorical indicators, you don't need to estimate the polychoric correlation matrix.  You just use the "ordered" argument to tell lavaan which variables are categorical, and it will use the appropriate steps by default.

messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan-group,

I´m still working on a SEM consisting of

-       four latent exogeneous variables (1 single-item indicator (see Yves response here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/e9kXRtiL9lU/yn8d-l1H29sJ> or Kline, 2016), two LVs are at least measured by 3 indicators (5-point Likert-style items), one LV is measured by four metric indicators (derived from item-parcelling – I know, it´s “bad style”, but this is what is commonly accepted for this construct),
-       four endogenous latent variables (each LV measured by five 5-point Likert items)
-       as well as two binary observed outcomes (coded 0/1).

In a single-group analysis the model is already quite huge, df = 600. I do have a sample of 835 participants, consisting of two different groups. Having a look at histograms I see that the data is not always normal (as far as you can tell having ordinal indicators).

The goal is

a) to investigate the relationship between the exogenous variables and the endogenous variables

b) comparing the means of the endogenous LVs across both groups while controlling for the exogenous LVs

c) analyzing the impact of the endogenous LVs on the dichotomous outcome

Most of the analysis was carried out using the MLR estimator as I do have 5-point Likert items (Beauducel & Herzberg, 2006). In doing so I was not able to analyze c) within the SEM framework provided by lavaan as it does not support binary outcomes using the MLR estimator (which is different from Mplus. – I know that Yves is planning this for a future release of lavaan – afaik). So far I calculated factor scores to analyze c) by means of logistic regression within the glm() framework. But this seems to be a messy solution. For example, I don´t have many missings per item (usually below 1.3 % per indicator MAR) but predict() is not able to calculate factor scores for a case if there is a missing withing the manifest indicators in that case so I got a lot of NAs.

Using WLSMV brought me a lot of errors first, models did not converge and I got errors that said I had not enough cases for computing the gamma matrix (it might be that I forgot to code all my ordinal indicators as factor and, respectively didn´t use the order argument). Alternative estimators like the MML, which is able to handle dichotomous outcomes (as suggested by Yves here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/9wN4Z9pZ4ow/KhxFVr1tdsAJ>) took forever.

So because of the messy solution to analyze c) I tried the WLSMV estimator again and somehow it seems to work now. BUT there are a couple of questions arousing regarding the use of the WLSMV estimator I would be really happy when someone with more experience can help me with:

Question 1: Is there any other option to analyze c) within the SEM framework I might have overlooked?

Question 2: Using the WLSMV estimator I do get a list of 50 warnings which might related to the zero.cell.warn argument:

…

50: In pc_cor_TS(fit.y1 = FIT[[i]], fit.y2 = FIT[[j]], method = optim.method,  ... :

  lavaan WARNING: empty cell(s) in bivariate table of wdn.handlung.3 x i8.09

…

Can I ignore these warnings?

Question 3: I am using WLSMV with missing=pairwise. I have a really low amount of missings in my data set (0.2% - 1.39%). Is it still worth to multiple impute my data? Besides the fact that it takes a pretty long time to calculate, when I do run cfa.mi() I get a strange chi-squre p-value which is p = 0.66 with chi^2 = 2271 and df = 717. That does not make any sense to me. This doesn´t happen when I use missing=pairwise.I think that I want to keep it simple and therefore just use missing=pairwise. What would you suggest?

Question 4: The model fit produced by the MLR estimator and the WLSMV estimator differs. For example, I got a CFI of 0.93 with the MLR estimator and a CFI of .92 with the WLSMV estimator. Sometimes it is the other way around and sometimes the difference is bigger. I think this is neglectable, right?

Question 5: The standardized regression coefficients (and correlations) vary. For example, using MLR as estimations method, a  standardized regression coefficient in my model is .26, using WLSMV it is .49. This is a big difference. Is there any particular reason for it? Kline (2016, p. 258) refers to a study where robust WLS estimation failed to perform well when distributions on categorical indicators are markedly skewed (But is robust WLS the same as WLSMV?).  I know that the indicators for this LV are skewed a little bit. On the other hand he says: “In general, ML estimates and their standard errors may both be too low when the data analyzed are from categorical indicators, and the degree of this negative bias is higher as distributions of items responses become increasingly non-normal (p. 257). In addition Brown (2006) states that “treating categorical variables in CFA are multifold, including that it can (1) produce attenuated estimates of the relationships (correlations) among indicators, especially when there are floor or ceiling effects. […] d) produce incorrect standard errors. Is there any new research on the efficacy of WLSMV vs. MLR by non-normal, ordinal indicators? What would you as

Question 6: What is best practice for the parametrization argument? Until now, I left it to default, although ?cfa doesn´t state what´s the default (theta or delta). As far as I know, delta scaling fixes the total variance of the LV to 1.0, which is not what I want as I want to compare different groups and I can not assume that the variance of the LV between both groups is equal.

Question 7: Using MLR I yielded two significant differences in the endogenous latent variables across the groups. Now, using WLSMV all four differences on latent means are significant with meaningful effect size. Does WLSMV have so much more power? How can I justify these “new” effects ?

Question 8: Are dichotomous outcomes modeled by probit link functions using WLSMV ? I know that there is a way to rescale the results from probit regression to Odds Ratios like in Logit regression for much easier interpretation. Is that meaningful here?

Question 9: Is my sample size big enough?

On Tuesday, May 10, 2016 at 9:55:14 AM UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> Jesus,
>
> I think "local identification" is a heuristic.  A model is either globally identified or not, and if it is not, then you look for clues about which part of the model might not be "locally" identified so you can solve the problem.  Identification can depend on aspects of your data, not just counting the number of free parameters and observed sample moments.  A 2-indicator CFA by itself is not identified without the constraints such as the ones you used (or, for example, fixing both factor loadings to 1 and estimating the common factor variance and both unique factor variances).  But when you have multiple 2-indicator constructs in a model, it can be identified (i.e., a unique solution can be found), as long as the constructs correlate.  Steiger illustrates this in the first section of this article:
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//1082-989X.7.2.210
>
> I didn't see any evidence of empirical underidentification in your original model, but the model with equal factor loadings fits poorly and yields estimates at the border ("Heywood cases").  So I would recommend trusting the results from the less constrained model in your original post.  But I also agree with Ed that factor score indeterminacy is an important limitation to using factor scores.  If you were planning to use the factor scores in a subsequent model, you would probably be better off just incorporating that model into this model to estimate those parameters (assuming the model is not so large that your small sample size becomes a limiting factor).

messages.body_plain:
> it is highly impornat that I link the factor scores back to the the correct 'participant-IDs'.  I utilized the following code to predict the factor scores.
>
> #FactorScores <- predict(fit_Model)
>
> However lavaan calculates 1218 facor scores and I have 1403 participants in my data set.

If you are using FIML for missing data, lavaan will return NAs for the appropriate rows, but you would still have fewer factor scores than rows if there are any rows that are missing all variables in the model.  If that is the case, it would be easier to create a copy of the data set without those rows:

> modelVarNames <- fit_Model@pta$vnames$ov
> allAreMissing <- apply(originalData[ , modelVarNames], 1, function(x) all(is.na <http://is.na>(x)) )
> myData <- originalData[ !allAreMissing , ]

Then (assuming you have a single-group model) use the approach linked here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/mf9WVimJFLY/36I-T2XbAAAJ>.  If you have a multiple-group model, predict() will return a list of data.frames (one per group) instead of a single data frame with a column for the grouping variable (as you saw in this post <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/Q2vrq5NbuNw/VsRClL2sAQAJ>).  So you could sort the data by the grouping variable, then fit your model and save the output of predict(..., newdata), then stack the groups factor scores and merge them with the data.frame

> myData <- myData[ order(myData$groupVariable) , ]
> fit_Model <- lavaan(...)
> FactorScores <- do.call(rbind, predict(fit_Model, newdata = myData))
> myData <- cbind(myData, FactorScores)

Yes

> In the lavaan tutorial, it is indeed reported that "If you have no full dataset, but you do have a sample covariance matrix, you can still fit your model." (http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cov.html)

That page says nothing about robust estimation.  The example there assumes data are normally distributed.

> My data is measured on an ordinal scale with 5 levels. I tried to use WLSMV, but did not have a sample big enough for the solution to converge (WARNING: number of observation too small to compute Gamma).Therefore, my best second choice was MLM and I treated the scale like a continuous one, even if this can be criticized. In your previous post, you were using the "cut" function to turn SAS_DATA into ordered categories.  I hope you are not doing that to your actual observed data.  If your actual data is continuous, leave it that way.  This research <http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf> suggests you can get good estimates of structural parameters (e.g., factor correlations) when using robust MLE with ordinal indicators if they have at least 5 categories.  But your research is about the measurement model, and that same article shows that more than 5 categories would be necessary for good estimates of factor loadings.  If you can't even run WLSMV because of your small sample and you can't get more data, then you should be aware (and make your readers aware) that the ML estimates are probably attenuated.

messages.subject_clean: WLSMV vs. MLR in a model with 4 exogenous LVs, 4 endogenous LVs and a binary observed outcome
messages.body_plain:
> Question 1: Is there any other option to analyze c) within the SEM framework I might have overlooked?

Not that I am aware of, but try posting your questions on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>.  It is a much more general forum with a much wider audience of SEM experts, and for the most part, your questions are not specific to lavaan software.

> Question 2: Using the WLSMV estimator I do get a list of 50 warnings which might related to the zero.cell.warn argument:...Can I ignore these warnings?

You were using robust ML because almost all your variables have 5+ categories, except for the binary outcome.  When you switch to WLSMV, do you then start treating those 5-category Likert items as ordered as well as the binary outcome?  That probably explains why you observe the parameter differences in Questions 5 & 7.  I would be inclined to try fitting the model with DWLS and only treating the binary outcome as ordered, but I'm not sure how robust the "robust" column is when treating 5-category items as continuous.  That would be something to ask on SEMNET as well.

> Question 3: I am using WLSMV with missing=pairwise. I have a really low amount of missings in my data set (0.2% - 1.39%)... What would you suggest?

It's not preferable, but given the small amount of missingness, I wouldn't expect results to differ greatly between pairwise deletion and multiple imputation (or robust FIML).

> Question 4: The model fit produced by the MLR estimator and the WLSMV estimator differs. ... I think this is neglectable, right?

They are different estimators, and you are also fitting the model to different data (treating indicators as continuous v. ordered yields different df and sample moments), so you can't expect fit to be the same.  Technically, the MLR model is fundamentally misspecified, so it doesn't make sense to interpret those fit measures anyway.

> Question 6: What is best practice for the parametrization argument? Until now, I left it to default, although ?cfa doesn´t state what´s the default (theta or delta). As far as I know, delta scaling fixes the total variance of the LV to 1.0, which is not what I want as I want to compare different groups and I can not assume that the variance of the LV between both groups is equal.

The default is delta, and that has nothing to do with setting the LV (factor) variance to 1.0 (that is the "std.lv <http://std.lv>" argument).  The delta parameterization fixes residual variances of each latent item response to 1.0 (in the first group), and theta parameterization fixes the total variances of each latent item response to 1.0 (in the first group).  But in either parameterization, constraining loadings and thresholds across groups allows the latent item response (residual) variances to be estimated in all other groups.  Millsap & Yu-Tein (2004) recommended using theta for testing measurement invariance, which you need to do before running your regression model, so you should probably use theta (see examples here <http://sunthud.com/catInvariance.html>).

> Question 7: Using MLR I yielded two significant differences in the endogenous latent variables across the groups. Now, using WLSMV all four differences on latent means are significant with meaningful effect size. Does WLSMV have so much more power? How can I justify these “new” effects ?

As you quoted in Question 5, effects are attenuated when treating categorical data as continuous.  Treating them appropriately should give you more power.  Compare a Pearson correlation between 2 binary/ordered items to a polychoric correlation between the same items, and the polychoric will always be at least as large because of the additional information in its assumption about the underlying normal continuum.

> Question 8: Are dichotomous outcomes modeled by probit link functions using WLSMV ? I know that there is a way to rescale the results from probit regression to Odds Ratios like in Logit regression for much easier interpretation. Is that meaningful here?

Yes (probit by default), and if you have formulas for transforming probit slopes to logit slopes, then those should apply here too.

> Question 9: Is my sample size big enough?

Depends how big your group sizes are.  Robust DWLS needs bigger N than robust ML for estimates to stabilize.

> #Regressions
>
> int+exp+mu+evi~fw+wdn+si

Both lines below are redundant with the line above, with already regresses the outcomes "int" and "evi" on the predictor "fw", as well as the outcomes "exp" and "mu" on the predictor "wdn".  Every variable on the lefthand side of the "~" operator is regressed on every variable on the righthand side.

> int+evi~fw
>
> exp+mu~wdn
>
> #indirect effect
>
> fw+si+wdn~nfc
>
> Hyp.Post.richtig~evi+mu #Hyp.Post.richtig is the observed binary outcome

These regressions don't match your description of the model.  You said there are 4 exogenous LVs, but the only exogenous LV in your syntax (i.e., without any predictors) is "nfc".

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: effect size of latent mean differences
messages.subject_clean: effect size of latent mean differences
messages.body_plain:
> I want to calculate effect sizes of latent mean differences. Factor variances have been shown to be equal in both groups. For my measurement invariance analysis I used fixed variances for model identification (instead of fixing factor loadings).

If the effect size you want is Cohen's D, then you have it easy.  If latent variances are fixed to 1 in both groups, then differences between estimated latent means are already standardized mean differences.  Assuming the latent mean is fixed to 0 in the first group, any other group's estimated latent mean is the standardized mean difference of that group from Group 1 (because any mean minus zero is the same number).

> But for effect size I need the factor variances, therefore I computed the same model but with fixed factor loadings instead of fixed factor variances.

This is not necessary.  Fixing the latent variances does not mean that the variances do not exist; it means that they are equal to 1, which makes calculations easier because the denominator of Cohen's D is 1 (so you only need the numerator, which is the mean difference).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

In a second-order CFA, the first-order latent variables are 'middle-man'
variables. They are neither purely 'endogenous', or purely 'exogenous',
ie they are not listed in the output of lavNames(fit, "lv.y") or
lavNames(fit, "lv.x"). For these cases, lavaan -by default- does not add
correlations between the residual variances. Therefore, orthogonal =
TRUE has not effect, because there are no correlations between factors
to fix to zero. They are already zero.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running a MIMIC model in lavaan. The structure of the scripts is as following:

mimic <- fit.mimic = " F =~  X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6;
                                 F ~  Y1 + Y2;
                                 X1 ~~ X3;
                                 X3 ~~ X5"

fit <- cfa (mimic, data, estimator = MLR)
or
fit1 <- cfa(mimic, data, ordered = "X1", estimator = WLSMV)

in my data, X1 is binary, and my sample size is about 50. I tried both MLR and WLS (with set X1 as ordered, i.e. ordered = “ X1"), the results are really different. The MLR did not detect any significant relationships, while  WLS found many. I would like to ask which estimator I should use.

I read the book by Finch and French (Latent variable modelling in R, 2015), they mentioned if the data do not reach the assumption of multivariate normality, it is better to use WLS or its friends (WLSMV). And my data are not multivariate normal from Mardia test, as follow.

Mardia's Multivariate Normality Test
---------------------------------------
   data : dataset

   g1p            : 107.5234
   chi.skew       : 1021.472
   p.value.skew   : 1.128484e-06

   g2p            : 301.5029
   z.kurtosis     : 2.123852
   p.value.kurt   : 0.03368251

   chi.small.skew : 1081.817
   p.value.small  : 1.032461e-09

   Result          : Data are not multivariate normal.

Also about residual covariances, I used MI to decide the inclusion and exclusion of the residual covariances. I found different set of residual covariances significantly affect the model fit. Is there any standard to keep the residual covariance, if the MI is bigger than 3.8, while we did expect the relationship between the variables ?

Thank you a lot!

> > Question 2: Using the WLSMV estimator I do get a list of 50 warnings which might related to the zero.cell.warn argument:...Can I ignore these warnings?
>
> You were using robust ML because almost all your variables have 5+ categories, except for the binary outcome.  When you switch to WLSMV, do you then start treating those 5-category Likert items as ordered as well as the binary outcome?

Yes, exactly.

>  That probably explains why you observe the parameter differences in Questions 5 & 7.  I would be inclined to try fitting the model with DWLS and only treating the binary outcome as ordered, but I'm not sure how robust the "robust" column is when treating 5-category items as continuous.  That would be something to ask on SEMNET as well.
>
> > Question 3: I am using WLSMV with missing=pairwise. I have a really low amount of missings in my data set (0.2% - 1.39%)... What would you suggest?
>
> It's not preferable, but given the small amount of missingness, I wouldn't expect results to differ greatly between pairwise deletion and multiple imputation (or robust FIML).

Yes, that´s what I think too.

>
> > Question 4: The model fit produced by the MLR estimator and the WLSMV estimator differs. ... I think this is neglectable, right?
>
> They are different estimators, and you are also fitting the model to different data (treating indicators as continuous v. ordered yields different df and sample moments), so you can't expect fit to be the same.  Technically, the MLR model is fundamentally misspecified, so it doesn't make sense to interpret those fit measures anyway.
>
> > Question 6: What is best practice for the parametrization argument? Until now, I left it to default, although ?cfa doesn´t state what´s the default (theta or delta). As far as I know, delta scaling fixes the total variance of the LV to 1.0, which is not what I want as I want to compare different groups and I can not assume that the variance of the LV between both groups is equal.
>
> The default is delta, and that has nothing to do with setting the LV (factor) variance to 1.0 (that is the "std.lv <http://std.lv>" argument).

Yeah, here I was wrong. Of course I did not mean the variance of the latent variable, but the latent response variable.

>  The delta parameterization fixes residual variances of each latent item response to 1.0 (in the first group), and theta parameterization fixes the total variances of each latent item response to 1.0 (in the first group).

I read Kline´s Chapter on modeling with ordinal indicators and found a confusing statement "In delta scaling (parameterization), the total variance of the latent response variables is fixed to 1.0." (p.326) What is correct now? Anyway, I will pick theta for the analysis of measurement invariance. As far as I know now the only impact is on the unstandardized solution, right?

> > Question 8: Are dichotomous outcomes modeled by probit link functions using WLSMV ? I know that there is a way to rescale the results from probit regression to Odds Ratios like in Logit regression for much easier interpretation. Is that meaningful here?
>
> Yes (probit by default), and if you have formulas for transforming probit slopes to logit slopes, then those should apply here too.

I thought this would be easy, but couldn´t even find a relation it in the multiple regression bible by Cohen, Cohen, West & Aiken. There are discussions on CrossValidated where people multiply probits by 1.7 or 1.8 to get a logit which seems weird to me as in the non-linear regressions don´t have constant marginal effects.

>
> > Question 9: Is my sample size big enough?
>
> Depends how big your group sizes are.  Robust DWLS needs bigger N than robust ML for estimates to stabilize.

It is about 410 in each group. Until now, everything is converging fine.

>
> > #Regressions
> >
> > int+exp+mu+evi~fw+wdn+si
>
> Both lines below are redundant with the line above, with already regresses the outcomes "int" and "evi" on the predictor "fw", as well as the outcomes "exp" and "mu" on the predictor "wdn".  Every variable on the lefthand side of the "~" operator is regressed on every variable on the righthand side.
>
> > int+evi~fw
> >
> > exp+mu~wdn

Again, this was my mistake. There are some "#" missing in the codes.

> >
> > #indirect effect
> >
> > fw+si+wdn~nfc
> >
> > Hyp.Post.richtig~evi+mu #Hyp.Post.richtig is the observed binary outcome
>
> These regressions don't match your description of the model.  You said there are 4 exogenous LVs, but the only exogenous LV in your syntax (i.e., without any predictors) is "nfc".

Again, my mistake.  The original theory said there are 4 exogenous LV,  but nfc is so highly correlated to the other 3 exogenous LV that I can reasonably modify the model to use nfs to explain the other three, which makes a lot of sense.

Two more things regarding modeling with ordinal indicators:
1.  In the Handbook of Structural Equation Modeling by Hoyle on page 207 is written, that adding an ordinal outcome (as a regression) is equivalent to include another indicator in the measurement model of the LV on which the outcome is regressed on, and therefore, the meaning of the LV changes.  This is not the fact in classical (multiple) regression analysis, right? Given a simple hypothetical model where a factor "health" is measured by indicators like "age", "smoking" and "weight" which are all proven to have an impact on health. When the binary outcome "death" is regressed on illness, which makes sense in a particular way, technically "death" is treated as an indicator for health. How does that make conceptually sense?

2. Given the output of my model above for the binary outcome:

 Hyp.Post.richtig ~            est    std.err   z         p       std
    evi                      0.214    0.081    2.655    0.008    0.179    0.179
    mu                      -0.592    0.162   -3.658    0.000   -0.309   -0.309

According to this page <http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/stata/output/Stata_Probit.htm>, the predicted probability for Hyp.Post.richtig being 1 is

P=F(evi*0.214+mu*-0.592)), where F is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. But on which metric is evi and mu considered? I think it is not on the item-metric where I can then put in scores from 1-5, because evi and mu are latent variables.
I think, that this is the underlying latent response metric which is different from the original metric and not interpretable? Where is the intercept? Is it estimated to be zero? But that would mean, that if mu and evi are both zero, one still had a probability of getting Hyp.Post.richtig=1 of pnorm(0) = 50%, right? Where is my misunderstanding?

Terrence, you pointed out here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/zDcHbOnxdRg/tojfozDzFvAJ>, that one could generate predicted values of the outcome for certain levels of the predictors, but the predictors are latent variables here, how can I get representative values?

Logits were so much easier ;-)

Thank you!

messages.subject: Ordered Probit Model - Comparison of STATA with Lavaan (or MPLUS)
messages.subject_clean: Ordered Probit Model - Comparison of STATA with Lavaan (or MPLUS)
messages.body_plain:
Hello All - I posted a similar message on SEMNET and apologies to those who are subscribed to that mailing list also.

I want to estimate a bivariate ordered probit model. Outcome/Endogenous variables y(1) and y(2) are ordinal. I have a host of x-vars x(1) to x(n).

Lavaan ESTIMATION: Estimation in Lavaan can be done using the following code

Model <- '
               y(1) ~ x(1) + x(2) + x(3) + ... x(n) ;
               y(2) ~ x(1) + x(2) + x(3) + ... x(n) ;

               y(1) ~~  y(2)
'
The model is estimated using the WLSMV estimator. As discussed in Finney and DiStefano 2013 (pp 460), the WLSMV estimator to be minimized measures the distance between sample observed latent correlations and model estimated correlations (r-p) and weighted by the diagonal of the asymptotic covariance matrix. F(WLSMV) = (r-p)W(-1)(r-p)

STATA ESTIMATION: I could also estimate the exact same model in STATA using either the bioprobit module (Sajaia undated;  http://www.adeptanalytics.org/download/ado/bioprobit/bioprobit.pdf) which uses the Maximum Likelihood estimator (equation 6 & 7). This estimator, as detailed in the vignette, calculates the log likelihood based on model estimated probabilities multiplied by an indicator function which turns on and off based on the actual observation.

The mathematical form of the ML function as given in the STATA documentation seems very different from the mathematical form of ML estimator given in Finney and DiStefano. In the latter, the ML function is the trace of the residual covariance matrix.

MY QUESTIONS: Are the two estimators equivalent? How does estimation of an ordered probit model differ between Lavaan / MPLUS  and STATA. IS there a difference in interpretation of the two alternate estimates?

Thanks for your time

Gouri

messages.body_plain:
> And one more question: Is there any way to compare non-nested models using WLSMV? As far as I know, it is not possible to calculate Information criterions like AIC and BIC, right?

Correct, information criteria are calculated from likelihoods, so they aren't available using least-squares estimators.  The only test statistics for comparing non-nested models that I am aware of are also calculated from (casewise) likelihoods.  This isn't a lavaan-specific question, so you can post on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>, but I think your only option might be incremental fit indices (e.g., CFI).  If you can specify a single theoretically justifiable null model that is nested within all competing models (regardless of whether they are nested), then you can fit that model to your data and pass it to the fitMeasures() function (look at the "baseline.model" argument).  The resulting CFIs will all be somewhere on the same continuum between a null model and a saturated model (in which all models are nested, by definition).

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.8.1.16

messages.body_plain:
On 05/16/2016 04:26 AM, Gouri Shankar Mishra wrote:
> MY QUESTIONS: Are the two estimators equivalent?

Yes, very much so.

> How does estimation of
> an ordered probit model differ between Lavaan / MPLUS  and STATA.

For lavaan/Mplus, the default estimator is (D)WLS, using polychoric
correlations, thresholds and their asymptotic variance matrix as the
(inverted) weight matrix. STATA seems to use ML estimation, probably
using some sort of quadrature approach to integrate out the latent
variables. (in lavaan, you can get this by using estimator = "MML",
which is very, very slow, but otherwise perfectly ok with the probit
link; also in Mplus, you can use the ML estimator).

There is a ton of literature on the pros/cons between those two
approaches in different settings.

> there a difference in interpretation of the two alternate estimates?

If the model specification is the same, and both estimators are using
the probit link, the interpretation would be the same.

Yves.

> > Given the absolute fit of the configural model, does the following result indicate that the configural invariance does not exist (also, rmsea does exceed .06 (.062)? If this is the case, should the conclusion be that: the two groups do not have identical number and type of factors and/or the same set of significant loadings? >
> There is no simple diagnosis for why a configural model does not fit well.  It could be that the cross-loadings or correlated residuals exists in one group but not another, which would only necessitate freeing parameter but retaining the same basic structure.  But as you suggested, it might also indicate the groups have fundamentally different factor structures.
>
> Interestingly, the fit of the configural model does not just reflect group differences in model structure, but also overall model fit.  That is, you might have mediocre model fit, but the model might be equally (in)appropriate in both groups.  The semTools packages also has a function called permuteMeasEq(), which uses permutation methods to test configural invariance without confounding that test with overall model fit.  But that method has not yet been investigated much, so it is not clear whether you should try to address the overall fit of the model before or after testing configural invariance.  If you have any theoretically driven reasons to free certain parameters or posit competing models for your data, you should probably try fitting those models before using any data-driven techniques to tweak your model.

messages.body_plain:
> Question 1: Does anyone know which model is 'correct' in terms of classic multiple mediator models?

The "correct" model to fit would be the model that reflects your substantive theory about these variables are related.  Covariance structure models can take any form (subject to identification constraints), and the examples you read about are just that:  examples.

> Question 2: Or is it wrong to integrate a correlation in the model without adding it to the calculation of the mediation and the total effect?

Indirect paths are products of directed effects (single-headed arrows), not undirected relations (double-headed arrows).

> Question 3: Interestingly the models above reveal exactly the same results, despite for the beta value of the a2 and the c2 path. Even the values of the mediation and the total effect are exactly the same? How is that possible?

Your models are saturated because each variable is directly connected (via single- or double-headed arrows) to every other variable in the model, so I would expect chi-squared and df == 0 either way.  But unless the residual correlation between mediators == 0 (or a1 or b2 == 0), I would expect the indirect paths to differ by the quantity (a1*c2*b2).

But note that your syntax does not match your model.  You are regressing M2 on M1, not the other way around, so the actual indirect path in the model you actually fitted should be (a2*c2*b1).  Or you can leave it as it is but change "Mediator1 ~ c2*Mediator2" to "Mediator2 ~ c2*Mediator1" (and remove the redundant parameter two lines above it).

Also, your user-defined parameter "med" IS the total indirect effect of X on Y (i.e., you are summing all the indirect effects via the mediators).  The "total" calculation is correct, but your "total_indirect" calculation is not a meaningful quantity.

> Question 4: What I am also wondering about is, why the model with the c2 path does converge, whereas the model with the correlation instead of the c2 path does not converge?

Was there an error message about the syntax having a redundant parameter?  ("Mediator1 ~ c2*Mediator2" was specified twice in your syntax.)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> The test for the indirect effects is based on the Sobel test?

Yes, the delta method is used to derive SEs for user-defined parameters

> 1) Do I use bootstrapping ONLY to check the CI of the indirect effect or do I also report the CI of the regression coefficients?

You can, but bootstrapping has Monte Carlo error, so it won't perform as well as the normal-theory CIs for parameters whose sampling distributions are approximately normal.  (I think that even includes the indirect effect, if you have a large enough sample size for the product term to be approximately normal).

> 2) If I bootstrap, are the following sem-definitions specificed correct or do I miss something? (I don't have to specific test = "bootstrap" or test = "bollen.stine", since I already specified se = "boot")?

If you also want to use the Bollen-Stine bootstrap to test the null hypothesis of perfect fit, then you should add that option (otherwise you will only see the central chi-squared distribution p value in the summary() output); alternatively, you could just send your model to the bootstrapLRT function.  You can use the "ci = TRUE" argument to get regular percentile bootstrap CIs in the summary() output, or you can request the bias-corrected percentiles from the parameterEstimates() function.

> PS: are there any good and detailed tutorials on bootstrapped mediation in lavaan?

This page <http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/index.php?position=1x2x0#.Vz7OGvl95hE> has some slides Yves put together for mediation software, including a lot of information about lavaan.

messages.subject: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.subject_clean: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.body_plain:
To preface, this is my first foray into CFA and SEM, so please forgive me as I am likely making a number of unwitting mistakes.

I am currently working on a study to validate a proposed psychometric attitudinal scale. We have a number of indicator terms obtained from previous literature and from structured interviews (referred to here as x1 ... x21), and an idea of how these terms are related to a few latent factors (y1 ... y3).

Here is the lavaan model of those relationships:

cfa.model = "
    y1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9 + x10 + x11
    y2 =~ x12 + x13 + x14 + x15 + x16
    y3 =~ x17 + x18 + x19 + x20 + x21
"

We currently have a tiny sample of 20 responses and are hoping to move into full data collection in the very near future. However, going into it, we wanted to have an idea--aside from the numerous "rules of thumb" out there (i.e. 10-to-1 participants-to-indicators)--of the sample size required for our analyses. Here is a CSV containing the data, so you have an idea of what I am working with. <https://www.dropbox.com/s/5qr3yqnyxxi0nab/cfadata.csv?dl=0>

Looking into it, it seems like the best approach is CFA with a DWLS or WLSMV estimator, due to the properties of ordinal Likert-type data (Wang & Cunningham 2005 <http://www.amsciepub.com/doi/abs/10.2466/pr0.97.1.3-10>, and others). lavaan is unable to converge using either of these estimators on a data set so small, but does "succeed" using ML, for what it's worth. I am not sure if that is of any use.

So, following Beaujean 2014 <http://pareonline.net/getvn.asp?v=19&n=12>, I went to the simsem package to simulate some data and estimate the minimum sample size from there. I thought that using the distributions of the data we already have would be a good idea. However, when I run the following code, I end up with power estimates of 1.000 for everything aside from the factor-factor estimates, which are exceedingly small (< 0.05).

cfa.sim1 = sim(model=cfa.model, n=rep(c(200, 250, 300, 400, 500), 100),
          lavaanfun="cfa", realData=data, seed=555)
summaryParam(cfa.sim1)

The plotPower() function shows this doesn't change across the varying sample sizes. It wasn't entirely clear to me what simsem was using the realData argument for; whether it uses the distributions of both the indicators and the latent factors according to the model, or just the indicators. I also wasn't clear on why I would be getting 1.000 for all of the power estimates, though I assumed that the small sample size was causing it to fail because there simply wasn't enough information to estimate the distributions. I would be surprised if it were telling me that 200 was a more-than-adequate sample size, considering the number of indicators.

I then thought that, though less ideal, I could give it distributions with a moderate level of skewness (1.5) and kurtosis (3.0) [from Li 2015 <http://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13428-015-0619-7>] and go from there:

cfa.sim.dist = bindDist(p=3, skewness=1.5, kurtosis=3.0)
cfa.sim2 = sim(model=cfa.model, n=rep(c(200, 250, 300, 400, 500), 100),
           lavaanfun="cfa", facDist=cfa.sim.dist, seed=555)
summaryParam(cfa.sim2)

However, this still gives me the same power estimates as before (1.000 for all factor-indicator and indicator-indicator, < 0.05 for factor-factor). Do I also need to provide distributions for the indicators via the indDist argument, or does it generate these from the facDist distributions?

So, these are the questions I am currently faced with:
Is there a way to use the data set I have to estimate the distributions for the simulations and the power analysis, or is it simply too small to be useful?
If not, what is the best way to proceed? It seemed to fail even when provided with parameters for the factor distributions.
You may notice from the data set that there is a 'type' variable as well and that this is, in fact, a within-subjects design (each of the 5 participants rated 4 different samples). How do I incorporate this into my CFA model?
Thank you for any help.

However for the same model in lavaan the results are different - different estimates and a different fitted covariance matrix. I have checked the parameter specifications using the inspect function and they seem to be identical noting that the beta and gamma matrices are “joined” to a beta matrix, and phi and psi matrices  to a psi matrix. I suppose there is something wrong with my lavaan specification  - could you please tell me how to do? Below is the code.

Thanks in advance, Gunnar

LISREL code

TITLE RUN2 USING IMPLIED COV MATRIX FROM RUN1

 DA ni=6 no=200

 la

 PB FB A SN PBC I

 2.455      1.510      1.246      0.000      2.213      3.460
