messages.subject: Re: Interpretation CFA output
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation CFA output
messages.body_plain:
Your items are not very highly correlated - this might mean that they are measured with error, or it might mean that they are not measuring similar constructs.

That means that, by things like chi-square and RMSEA, your model is not very bad - but the trouble is that no models are especially bad. Try running a one factor model, it won't be very bad. In fact the null model, which proposes that there are no factors at all, is not very bad - your fitted model only reduces the chi-square by about half.

Your chi-square and RMSEA are good, because you don't have the power to find bad fit. That's why you should always look at CFI/TLI as well. (The reverse is true - very high CFI combined with poorer RMSEA/chi-square tells you that you had a lot of power. A conclusion you can draw is that CFI always works.)

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.subject_clean: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.body_plain:
> Looking into it, it seems like the best approach is CFA with a DWLS or WLSMV estimator, due to the properties of ordinal Likert-type data (Wang & Cunningham 2005 <http://www.amsciepub.com/doi/abs/10.2466/pr0.97.1.3-10>, and others). lavaan is unable to converge using either of these estimators on a data set so small, but does "succeed" using ML, for what it's worth. I am not sure if that is of any use.

It looks like your items have 7 catgories, in which case MLE sufficiently estimates factor loadings:

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

You can use MLR to correct SEs and test statistics for any non-normality, but the point estimates under ML should not be very attenuated with so many categories.

> 1. Is there a way to use the data set I have to estimate the distributions for the simulations and the power analysis, or is it simply too small to be useful?

A sample this small isn't going to allow you to have any confidence that parameter estimates will generalize to the population, but there is nothing wrong with using them as population parameters in a power analysis using simsem if you have no theoretical basis for choosing more plausible population values.

> 2. If not, what is the best way to proceed? It seemed to fail even when provided with parameters for the factor distributions.

I don't see how the power analysis could "fail", so I imagine you are talking about the real data.  You need more data.  Regarding rules of thumb for sample size (N), the number of items/parameters (model size) is not the only issue.  MacCallum et al. (1999) <http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.536.6317&rep=rep1&type=pdf> showed that there is an interaction between N, model size, and reliability/communality (how large the factor loadings are).  You can trust the results as long as 2 of those 3 factors are large, but two of those factors are small, the third factor would have to be huge to make up for the lack of information from the other two sources.  So the answer to your question, like so many other circumstances in applied statistics, is "it depends" -- in your case, it depends on how reliable your items are.  Y1 has lots of indicators, but Y2 and Y3 only have 5 each, so you should probably strive for N > 400 in case they are not composed mostly of common-factor variance.

> 3. You may notice from the data set that there is a 'type' variable as well and that this is, in fact, a within-subjects design (each of the 5 participants rated 4 different samples). How do I incorporate this into my CFA model?

Read about longitudinal CFA and multitrait-multimethod models for ideas about handling dependent measures like this.  Essentially, you can put the data in wide format (the same indicator will be in multiple columns, one for each within-subjects condition).  Then define the each factor separately for each condition (e.g., Factor1_type1, Factor2_type1, Factor1_type2, Factor2_type2) and also define a method factor for each indicator to account for item-specific variance that is constant across conditions.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
It sounds as if you have already figured out how to obtain modification indices using lavaan. If so, your question is not specific to lavaan and is probably too broad to allow a helpful reply on an email distribution list.

As a general rule, modifications indices should not be used in isolation but instead considered along with other information in a broader process of model respecification.  Modification indices estimate the improvement in chi-square expected if a fixed parameter were freely estimated.

Rex Kline's introductory SEM book contains material on model respecification including the use of modification indices, scattered across several chapters.  Both terms appear in the subject index.  The book also provides references to additional literature.

Kline, R. B. (2016).  Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (4th ed.).  New York:  Guilford.

Keith Markus

On Sunday, May 22, 2016 at 9:26:07 AM UTC-6, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > Looking into it, it seems like the best approach is CFA with a DWLS or WLSMV estimator, due to the properties of ordinal Likert-type data (Wang & Cunningham 2005 <http://www.amsciepub.com/doi/abs/10.2466/pr0.97.1.3-10>, and others). lavaan is unable to converge using either of these estimators on a data set so small, but does "succeed" using ML, for what it's worth. I am not sure if that is of any use.
>
> It looks like your items have 7 catgories, in which case MLE sufficiently estimates factor loadings:
>
> http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf
>
> You can use MLR to correct SEs and test statistics for any non-normality, but the point estimates under ML should not be very attenuated with so many categories.
>
> > 1. Is there a way to use the data set I have to estimate the distributions for the simulations and the power analysis, or is it simply too small to be useful?
>
> A sample this small isn't going to allow you to have any confidence that parameter estimates will generalize to the population, but there is nothing wrong with using them as population parameters in a power analysis using simsem if you have no theoretical basis for choosing more plausible population values.
>
> > 2. If not, what is the best way to proceed? It seemed to fail even when provided with parameters for the factor distributions.
>
> I don't see how the power analysis could "fail", so I imagine you are talking about the real data.  You need more data.  Regarding rules of thumb for sample size (N), the number of items/parameters (model size) is not the only issue.  MacCallum et al. (1999) <http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.536.6317&rep=rep1&type=pdf> showed that there is an interaction between N, model size, and reliability/communality (how large the factor loadings are).  You can trust the results as long as 2 of those 3 factors are large, but two of those factors are small, the third factor would have to be huge to make up for the lack of information from the other two sources.  So the answer to your question, like so many other circumstances in applied statistics, is "it depends" -- in your case, it depends on how reliable your items are.  Y1 has lots of indicators, but Y2 and Y3 only have 5 each, so you should probably strive for N > 400 in case they are not composed mostly of common-factor variance.
>
> > 3. You may notice from the data set that there is a 'type' variable as well and that this is, in fact, a within-subjects design (each of the 5 participants rated 4 different samples). How do I incorporate this into my CFA model?
>
> Read about longitudinal CFA and multitrait-multimethod models for ideas about handling dependent measures like this.  Essentially, you can put the data in wide format (the same indicator will be in multiple columns, one for each within-subjects condition).  Then define the each factor separately for each condition (e.g., Factor1_type1, Factor2_type1, Factor1_type2, Factor2_type2) and also define a method factor for each indicator to account for item-specific variance that is constant across conditions.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
Please can someone check my syntax - I imagine I'm close but the model doesn't run.
I am trying to predict (using regression) a latent outcome variable from a latent predictor variable (I have done this in SPSS; this analysis is designed to model variables as latent variables in order to remove measurement error). I am trying to test for nonlinear effects, comparing 3 models that have indicators that respectively consist of (1) the raw item scores, (2) squared item scores, and (3) cubed item scores. I would like to compare the fit of the 3 models, akin to something like R squared change. I understand that there is no need to define covariances between latent variables as "all exogenous latent variables are correlated by default" in Lavaan. My syntax is below. Any help would be really appreciated!!

library(foreign)

STAI <- read.dta("c:/Users/Laptop/Desktop/Hawaiianfile.dta")

library(lavaan)

model <- '

# latent variable definitions

STAI =~ trait1 + trait2 + trait3 + trait4 + trait5 + trait6 + trait7 + trait8 + trait9 + trait10 + trait11 + trait12 + trait13 + trait14 + trait15 + trait16 + trait17 + trait18 + trait19 + trait20

STAISQUARED =~ trait1SQUARED + trait2SQUARED + trait3SQUARED + trait4SQUARED + trait5SQUARED + trait6SQUARED + trait7SQUARED + trait8SQUARED + trait9SQUARED + trait10SQUARED + trait11SQUARED + trait12SQUARED + trait13SQUARED + trait14SQUARED + trait15SQUARED + trait16SQUARED + trait17SQUARED + trait18SQUARED + trait19SQUARED + trait20SQUARED

STAICUBED =~ trait1CUBED + trait2CUBED + trait3CUBED + trait4CUBED + trait5CUBED + trait6CUBED + trait7CUBED + trait8CUBED + trait9CUBED + trait10CUBED + trait11CUBED + trait12CUBED + trait13CUBED + trait14CUBED + trait15CUBED + trait16CUBED + trait17CUBED + trait18CUBED + trait19CUBED + trait20CUBED

CESD =~ dep_1 + dep_2 + dep_3 + dep_4 + dep_5 + dep_6 + dep_7 + dep_8 + dep_9 + dep_10 + dep_11 + dep_12 + dep_13 + dep_14 + dep_15 + dep_16 + dep_17 + dep_18 + dep_19 + dep_20’

# regressions

CESD ~ STAI + STAISQUARED + STAICUBED

fit <- sem(model, data = STAI)

summary(fit, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Can you explain what you mean by "the model doesn't run."

I think your problem might be this. Consider just this:

STAI =~ trait1 + trait2

STAISQUARED =~ trait1SQUARED + trait2SQUARED

STAICUBED =~ trait1CUBED + trait2CUBED

According to the model, the only reason that trait1, trait1sq and trait1cu correlate is because the latent variables they indicate are correlated. But variables tend to be (very) highly correlated with their square and cube so this model is likely very badly misspecified.

jeremy

messages.subject_clean: Help with confidence intervals for standardised regression coefficients
messages.body_plain:
> Does anyone know how to compute the CIs for the standardised regression coefficients from my model fit?

You should use unstandardized coefficients for making inferences about a null hypothesis, and use standardized coefficients as a standardized measure of effect size.  But if you just want to use the width of a CI (or just the size of the SE) to describe the sampling variability you would expect for a standardized coefficient across repeated experiments, then you can get the SE from the standardizedSolution() function, and calculate a central normal-theory CI from that.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I'm not sure how it could be the same problem because read.spss() doesn't need a header argument; SPSS data files don't put their variables in the first row, like text or Excel files do.  Are you talking about the having unordered factors that should be numeric (like scales whose points were labeled in the SPSS file)?  In that case, you set use.value.labels = FALSE and use the factor() or ordered() function to assign levels to nominal/ordinal factors if you have any. messages.subject: Re: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.subject_clean: CFA power analysis using existing Likert-type (ordinal) data
messages.body_plain:
> ...(1.000 power for nearly all comparisons). Do you have any idea what could be going wrong, or are the results actually accurate (N=200 sufficient for power analysis), or am I misinterpreting the output?

Hard to know if that should be surprising.  By comparisons, I assume you are talking about a likelihood ratio test (chi-squared difference between nested models).  If you put your population values into matrices (like you do for the popParam argument in simsem::bind), you can calculate the population mean vector and covariance matrix using matrix algebra.  Then fit any model to the population moments using the sample.cov and sample.means arguments (setting sample.nobs to any arbitrary value).  Then you can extract the model-implied moments from the model fit, and use simsem::popDiscrepancy() to calculate population-level discrepancy measures (RMSEA, SRMR, and minimum ML fit function) of the model.

> M1 <- intercepts + Lambda %*% Alpha
> S1 <- Lambda %*% Psi %*% t(Lambda) + Theta
> fit0 <- lavaan(model, sample.cov = S1, sample.means = M1, sample.nobs = 200)
> M0 <- lavInspect(fit0, "mean.ov")
> S0 <- lavInspect(fit0, "cov.ov")
> popDiscrepancy(paramM = M1, paramCM = S1, misspecM = M0, misspecCM = S0)

That takes sampling error out of the equation and let's you see a descriptive measure of model misfit.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: group.equal="thresholds" (categorical data measurement invariance) appears to not be acting properly
messages.subject_clean: group.equal="thresholds" (categorical data measurement invariance) appears to not be acting properly
messages.body_plain:
> So doesn't this mean that the scalar invariance model is not nested within the metric invariant model?
>
> If I am thinking about this correctly, the metric invariance model constrains the loading and scale parameters but the scalar invariance model constrains the loadings and thresholds but now frees the scaling in the second group.

The idea of parameter nesting gets very tricky when thresholds are part of the model, because thresholds are related to both the location and scale of the variables (mean and covariance structure of the model), as opposed to means and covariance structure being independent of entities with MV-normal data.  Millsap & Yun-Tien (2004) provide an excellent discussion of how to test measurement invariance using minimal constraints:

http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1207/S15327906MBR3903_4

Although I forget how clearly they describe the nesting of models, I know they show that you cannot discriminate between metric and scalar invariance with only binary items.  If thresholds differ across groups/time, it could be because the mean of the latent response differs, or the variance differs (or both), but there is not enough information to distinguish which.  So differences in factor loadings will not be able to show poor fit because that misspecification can just be re-expressed as a difference in thresholds.  Not sure if this is your situation, but it's just an example of how thresholds make things less intuitive, so parameter-counting heuristics might not apply like the do to continuous data.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

"Yes, the chi-square difference testing is fine and H0 is nested within H1. This is so even though H0 has Delta and factor mean parameters free that H1 doesn't have. messages.subject: Re: Unconstraining single items in measurementInvariance()
messages.subject_clean: Unconstraining single items in measurementInvariance()
messages.body_plain:
> However, instead of excluding, is it possible to unconstrain the items in the model or the measurementInvariance() command to keep the items unconstrained across groups?

That might be a more ideal way to handle it.  Excluding items is only justified if you conclude they do not measure the underlying construct.  An item could still be a valid measure even if the way it is associated with the underlying construct differs across particular populations.  But it depends whether you intend to model that construct using latent-variable models or intend to use a scale sum/mean as a proxy for the construct.

This isn't software specific, so you should consider posting a general SEM question like this on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>, which has a larger audience of SEM experts.  But if you need to know how to free item parameters across groups in lavaan, it depends how you impose the constraints.  If you use labels in the syntax, just give the parameters different labels.  But if you use the "group.equal" argument, you can provide exceptions of particular parameters to NOT constrain to equality, using the "group.partial" argument.

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I think the partialInvariance() function could serve your purpose. The resulting lavaan object can be extracted from the function. For example,

library(lavaan)

conf <- "
f1 =~ NA*x1 + x2 + x3
f2 =~ NA*x4 + x5 + x6
f1 ~~ c(1, 1)*f1
f2 ~~ c(1, 1)*f2
"

weak <- "
f1 =~ NA*x1 + x2 + x3
f2 =~ NA*x4 + x5 + x6
f1 ~~ c(1, NA)*f1
f2 ~~ c(1, NA)*f2
"

configural <- cfa(conf, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, group="school")
weak <- cfa(weak, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group="school", group.equal="loadings")
models <- list(fit.configural = configural, fit.loadings = weak)
outs <- partialInvariance(models, "metric", return.fit = TRUE)
outs$models

Dear Lavaan group,

I apologize in advance that this is not a strictly Lavaan question but would appreciate any suggestions from the group. Using Lavaan, I have completed the CFA of data involving ordinal variables (all based on same 5-pt likert scales). I came across the point that 5-level responses may be treated as continuous in a few posts that referenced Rhemtulla 2012 (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/kdbSKNRDiYg/O7nfRz0UBAAJ <http://psycnet.apa.org/?&fa=main.doiLanding&doi=10.1037/a0029315>) and ran the CFA treating the variables as both continuous and "ordered." The results differed to some extent, and I am now thinking that it may be worth backtracking and treat the data as ordered in both the PCA and EFA stages to compare the results (Also, many of the variables (particularly the initial item pool) show significant skew with only 5 item response options available)

I completed both PCA and EFA outside of R and would appreciate any packages or methods you may recommend for these steps. I have come across a few options based on my own search (e.g. MCA using FactoMineR or CATPCA in SPSS) but would appreciate input from those that may be more familiar. Alternatively, if I were to complete CFA with data as ordered, is it necessary preceding steps also accounted for the data as ordered?

Thank you.

messages.body_plain:
> I came across the point that 5-level responses may be treated as continuous in a few posts that referenced Rhemtulla 2012 (https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/kdbSKNRDiYg/O7nfRz0UBAAJ <http://psycnet.apa.org/?&fa=main.doiLanding&doi=10.1037/a0029315>) and ran the CFA treating the variables as both continuous and "ordered."

If your research interest is the measurement parameters, then your factor loadings will be attenuated with only 5 categories.  Read the recommendations in the paper carefully -- only the structural parameters are unbiased with 5 categories.  7 categories appear necessary for good estimates of factor loadings.

> I completed both PCA and EFA outside of R and would appreciate any packages or methods you may recommend for these steps.

I wouldn't recommend an exploratory model if you have any theory-driven hypotheses about what your items measure.  I certainly wouldn't use PCA if you hypothesize common factors (which PCA does not; PCA is an eigen decomposition, not a measurement model).  But if you don't know anything about what your items measure, you can perform EFA using lavaan.  In the semTools package, there is a function called efaUnrotate() that fits an EFA to your model using lavaan, so you can pass any lavaan() arguments to it (e.g., ordered, in which case it would choose DLWS estimation by default).  Then you can rotate the solution using oblqRotate().

messages.subject_clean: Selecting analyses with ordered variables
messages.body_plain:
Likert items are ordinal categorical, Likert scales are continuous.  It sounds as if you should use item response theory to convert the set of response to your items into estimates of values on the underlying Likert scale(s).  IRT will give you estimates and their standard errors.  You can then analyse these values as continuous.  Be sure to include the measurement errors in you analysis, or you will introduce bias.  see (Lu, I. R. R. 2005. Embedding IRT in structural equation models: A comparison with regression based on IRT scores. Structural Equation Modeling-a Multidisciplinary Journal 12:263-277.)  There are a number of R packages that will analyse Likert style data.  The one I am most familiar with is mirt.  Mirt is well documented and has an active user's group.

One more point to raise.  You mention skewed results.  This is only a problem if you have individuals all of whose responses are either the minimum or maximum.  In which case you have censored data even when converted to the Likert scale.  Censored data will also generate biases, which may be large (see Holst, K. K., T. H. Scheike, and J. B. Hjelmborg. 2016. The liability threshold model for censored twin data. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 93:324-335.)  The lavaan package doesn't yet handle censored data, but the lava package does. messages.subject: Re: interactions of indicators in path analysis
messages.subject_clean: interactions of indicators in path analysis
messages.body_plain:
Things to think about when interpreting your results.

1) even if X1 & X2 have mean 0, interaction12 does not.  it has a mean = cov(X1,X2).  This term will probably pop up in your intercept.  Or you can recenter interaction12 before entering it into your prediction of Y.
2) even if X1 & X2 have normally distributed errors, interaction12 will not.  it will be leptokurtic.  I would not rely on asymptotic standard errors for inference, but would instead suggest bootstrapping.  Of course, you have said this is a path analysis rather than a SEM analysis, implying that the Xs are known exactly (without error).  However, this is almost always a fantasy.

You might want to look at Coenders, G., J. M. Batista-Foguet, and W. E. Saris. 2008. Simple, efficient and distribution-free approach to interaction effects in complex structural equation models. Quality & Quantity 42:369-396.

And also Lin, G. C., Z. L. Wen, H. W. Marsh, and H. S. Lin. 2010. Structural Equation Models of Latent Interactions: Clarification of Orthogonalizing and Double-Mean-Centering Strategies. Structural Equation Modeling-a Multidisciplinary Journal 17:374-391.

Best MLT

messages.subject_clean: Selecting analyses with ordered variables
messages.body_plain:
The Likert items are your questions, the Likert scale is an estimate of an underlying continuous axis.  It corresponds to the factors in efa and cfa.  Like factor analysis IRT analysis can be either exploratory or confirmatory.

Do you need to redo the analysis?  That depends on what you plan on using it for, and what kind of time pressure your are under.  If you just need to take a quick look at the data before making some sort of decision about the design of future work, then the fa may be good enough.  If on the other hand, the fine details of the results matter, then you should do it over.

The big picture will probably be similar.  The fa is an approximation to the irt factor analysis based on assumptions about the data that we know to be false.  The irt factors will be similar to the fa factors, but they will be different. It is hard to say whether those differences will be important until you look at them.  There is also no question that the irt analysis will be more defensible for publication purposes.

Best MLT

Your R syntax stops after the character string with lavaan model syntax, and I don't think that would have produced the error, so I'm guessing you called sem() again after that? Use the ~~ operator to specify a (residual) covariance between any pair of variables (or a variance, which is a covariance of a variable with itself).

You can save the output of parameterEstimates() and extract the pvalues column, as long as you know which row to look for.

> params <- parameterEstimates(ModFitLV1)
> params$pvalue

Or you can print the parameterEstimates() output using the print() method with the nd argument (for up to 8 digits, I think).

> print(params, nd = 8)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

You can use:
clipboard(model_fit,fit.measures=TRUE,standardized=TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

Or if you just want the std.all regressionparameters:
pathcoeff<-parameterEstimates(model.fit, standardized=TRUE)[,c(1:3,5:8,12)] %>% filter(op == "=~")
pathcoeff<-as.data.frame(pathcoeff[,c(1:3,8)])

messages.subject: Re: Mediation SEM - error could not find function ":="
messages.subject_clean: Mediation SEM - error could not find function ":="
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thanks for your quick response- I think it was an issue with my syntax and not specifying all parts and it now works using the following commands:

SCTModel2 <- 'PF1=~pers2+pers4+pers3+pers8+pers7

BehF1=~BF1+BF2+BF3+BF4+BF6+BF7

EnvF1=~Env1+Env3+Env4+Env5

 # direct effect

             BehF1 ~ c*PF1

           # mediator

            EnvF1 ~ a*PF1

             BehF1 ~ b*EnvF1

           # indirect effect (a*b)

             ab := a*b

           # total effect

             total := c + (a*b)

         '

SCT2fit<-sem(SCTModel2, data = SMBI_Alldata, estimator="MLR", bootstrap = 5000)

summary(SCT2fit, standardized = T, fit.measures = T, rsq = T)

As you can see, I have used robust maximum likelihood estimation due to the lack of multivariate normality in my data (this is the approach that was recommended to me when I was doing confirmatory factor analysis using lavaan). However is this correct/ necessary in a mediation analysis, and should it be combined with the bootstrapping command like I've done above or not?

I used another command to perform bias corrected accelerated bootstrapping in order to get the confidence intervals for the indirect effect- as shown in my syntax below, but I'm not really sure what the difference is between the parameter estimates bootstrapping and the bootstrapping command I have used above?

> boot.fit <- parameterEstimates(SCT2fit, boot.ci.type="bca.simple",level=0.95, ci=TRUE,standardized = FALSE)

> boot.fit

I'd be really grateful for any help in trying to understand the approach to bootstrapping a little better.

In addition, are there any resources to help interpret the output of this mediation analysis? I'm not sure what parts I should be focusing on/writing up??

Thanks

Emma

Your R syntax stops after the character string with lavaan model syntax, and I don't think that would have produced the error, so I'm guessing you called sem() again after that?  What version of lavaan and R are you using?  You can copy/paste the output of sessionInfo() to show us.
>
> > Also, in many other examples I have seen residual variances and covariances included in the syntax but I don’t know how you determine/ decide on these?
>
> Use the ~~ operator to specify a (residual) covariance between any pair of variables (or a variance, which is a covariance of a variable with itself).
>
> http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html
>
> > If anyone has any suggestions of where I can find help with interpreting the output that would be really appreciated :)

> If the lavaan paper <https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v048i02> or tutorial pages <http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/index.html> don't have the information you need, this book <http://blogs.baylor.edu/rlatentvariable/> teaches SEM using lavaan, and this book <https://books.google.nl/books?id=cdEBCgAAQBAJ&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0#v=onepage&q&f=false> teaches latent variable models using lavaan for SEM and mirt for IRT.
